story.title: Trump Warns Iran Over Strait of Hormuz Deal Deadline
story.summary: Donald Trump stated that a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could be reached as early as Wednesday. He warned that if negotiations fail, Iran would face severe consequences. The situation follows Iran's increased control over the strait, where it has sought to impose tolls, a move not previously exercised before the conflict began on February 28.

He stated that for each ship fired upon by Iranian forces, the US would respond by destroying a corresponding piece of Iranian infrastructure. This escalation comes amid ongoing tensions in the region and rising oil prices.
key_facts: Trump threatened to destroy Iranian infrastructure for each ship attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The threat follows continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the region.
Oil prices have surged amid the escalating tensions.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict that began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel carried out strikes in Iran and Iran subsequently attacked U.S. military assets and regional states. It has expanded beyond direct military exchanges to include disputes over maritime access in the Strait of Hormuz, ceasefire efforts, and risks to commercial shipping and civilian seafarers.

facts.label: Start and principal belligerents
facts.value: The United Nations reported that U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran occurred on February 28, 2026; Iran then targeted U.S. military assets and attacks affected several regional states. In a subsequent Security Council letter, the United States said it had commenced combat operations against Iran that day in cooperation with Israel.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: A central theater is the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway between Iran and Oman linking the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. The conflict has also affected U.S. forces and states across the Gulf region.

facts.label: Maritime and legal dimension
facts.value: The International Maritime Organization has treated attacks on merchant shipping and restrictions on passage through Hormuz as a major international-shipping issue. Its Council stated that transit passage through straits used for international navigation must not be threatened, impeded, denied, or suspended, and that any traffic measures must accord with IMO rules and international law.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: Ceasefire and mediation efforts have occurred alongside renewed fighting. The UN described a June 17 memorandum of understanding and Qatar-facilitated implementation talks, while warning in early July that the arrangement remained fragile after further U.S.-Iran confrontations.

facts.label: Civilian shipping impact
facts.value: IMO said on June 15 that it had verified at least 46 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began, and it later organized a voluntary emergency framework to help vessels and seafarers confined in the Gulf depart safely.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the late-July 2026 escalation involving U.S. threats and strikes, congressional war-powers action, Houthi-linked developments, oil-market disruption, and a reported pause in attacks; it does not provide a complete record of the war’s origins, all regional operations, or the full course of diplomacy.

explore_lenses.label: What would the proposed shipping plan change?
explore_lenses.title: A temporary, managed transit arrangement
explore_lenses.summary: The draft described by regional officials would not simply restore the prewar status quo: it would assign separate inbound and outbound routes and permit service fees. It is presented as an interim arrangement, not a final settlement of the wider U.S.-Iran dispute.

claims.text: Two regional officials told AP that the draft would have ships enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman.
Those officials said service fees would be charged for security and maritime-environment protection, while Trump has publicly opposed Iranian tolls.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran's talks with Oman concern safe inbound and outbound lanes that preserve Iranian and Omani sovereign rights while addressing both countries' security concerns.

explore_lenses.label: How did Hormuz become the central issue?
explore_lenses.title: War and attacks choked a vital shipping route
explore_lenses.summary: The route dispute emerged from the conflict that began on February 28, then intensified as threats and attacks on shipping sharply reduced traffic. The stakes extend beyond the parties to the war because the strait had carried a major share of global oil and gas flows.

claims.text: AP reported that the United States and Israel began the war on February 28, and that Iranian threats and attacks on shipping subsequently brought traffic through the strait nearly to a halt.

The UN said on June 8 that ship transits had fallen by more than 90% since the crisis escalated in late February, and described the strait as a route for about one-quarter of global seaborne oil trade.
The UN secretary-general has called for restoration of navigational rights and freedoms in the strait under international law, while urging de-escalation and renewed diplomacy.

explore_lenses.label: What must happen before ships can reopen?
explore_lenses.title: Approval and implementation remain unresolved
explore_lenses.summary: A reported draft is not yet an operative agreement. Iran's supreme leader is reportedly the remaining approval point, while U.S. officials say progress does not mean the terms are final and attacks have continued near the route.

claims.text: Regional officials told AP that Iranian and Omani negotiators had finalized a draft, but that it was awaiting final approval from Iran's supreme leader.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said progress had been made but that the negotiations were not final; he has opposed an arrangement granting Iran control over the strait.
Forecast: Trump said an announcement could come on August 5 or August 6, 2026, but this was a presidential expectation rather than confirmation of a signed deal.
On August 5, a cargo ship reported being hit by an unknown projectile northeast of Al Khasab in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center as reported by AP.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could be announced as early as Wednesday and warned Iran of severe repercussions if negotiations fail. The comments coincided with reports that Iranian and Omani negotiators had finalized a draft governing passage through the waterway, though it still required final approval from Iran’s supreme leader. The immediate result is continued uncertainty for commercial shipping: no signed agreement, public draft text or verified timetable for safe transits has been released.

sections.heading: Iran-Oman Draft Terms
sections.body: Two regional officials told AP that the reported draft would route ships into the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled lane and out through a lane controlled by Oman. The officials said vessels would pay service fees for security and maritime-environment protection, a provision at odds with Trump’s public opposition to Iranian tolls. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei described talks with Oman as addressing safe inbound and outbound lanes while preserving both countries’ sovereign rights and security concerns.

sections.heading: Shipping Traffic and Security
sections.body: AP reported that Iranian threats and attacks on shipping after the war began February 28 brought traffic through the strait nearly to a halt, while the parties dispute responsibility for both the conflict and the maritime-security crisis. The United Nations said on June 8 that transits had fallen by more than 90% since the crisis escalated in late February and that the strait carries about one-quarter of global seaborne oil trade. On August 5, a cargo ship reported being struck by an unknown projectile northeast of Al Khasab, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center as reported by AP.

sections.heading: Approval and Navigation Rights
sections.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said progress had been made but negotiations were not final, and he opposed any arrangement that would give Iran control over the strait. Trump said an announcement could come on August 5 or August 6, but that was an expectation rather than confirmation of a completed agreement. The UN secretary-general has called for navigational rights and freedoms to be restored under international law, alongside de-escalation and renewed diplomacy.

unresolved.text: Iran and Oman had not officially commented on the reported draft terms, and no public text of the draft has been released.
It remains unresolved whether Iran’s supreme leader will grant final approval and when safe commercial transits could begin.

related_stories.title: Israeli Military Actions Challenge Trump's Gaza Peace Proposal
related_stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a recent peace proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump, which calls for the disarmament of Hamas and an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Netanyahu stated that the Israeli army will not retreat from its positions until Hamas is fully disarmed, contradicting the terms of a previous ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, reports indicate that Trump would be disappointed if Israel does not accept the new plan.
